outcome: No source found says the question has been settled either way since 26 January 2024, and nothing in the window moves it: the in-window items are a 2024 thesis that reports an unnamed attempted proof of infinitude is flawed, a 2025 paper on Mersenne-number conjectures, a 2026 Diophantine paper on k-Lucas numbers, a 2026 paper certifying primality of three exponents already on the known list, and computational probable-prime records. A 2019 viXra preprint claiming a proof of infinitude (Marshall) is pre-window and its text could not be opened, so it remains unassessed.
problem_asks: Single question: are there infinitely many Wagstaff primes, i.e. infinitely many primes of the form (2^p+1)/3 with p an odd prime? The statement does not spell out the definition; the standard reading (Wikipedia, OEIS A000978) takes p to range over odd primes, and this is the reading used throughout. Parts: (1) the set of Wagstaff primes is infinite. No sub-parts. The statement does not ask for the list of exponents, for counts up to x, for proven versus probable status of any value, or for the 1989 New Mersenne conjecture. Wikipedia's article also states, for the more general Q(b,n) = (b^n+1)/(b+1) with bases lacking algebraic factorisation, that it is conjectured infinitely many n give primes; that generalisation is not what this bullet asks.

events.what_happened: Alexey Dolotov (independent researcher) posted 'Three Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge primality proofs for Wagstaff numbers'. It gives unconditional BLS N-1 primality certificates for W_2617 (788 digits), W_10501 (3161 digits) and W_12391 (3730 digits), with every cofactor certified by APR-CL and a Chua-congruence sanity check. First public as a Zenodo deposit (v1.5.2, 18 Apr 2026, record 19644188; the deposit contains LaTeX manuscript sources in paper/, code and certificates), then as arXiv:2605.18555 (v1, 18 May 2026, math.NT, 11 pages). Code and certificates MIT; manuscript CC-BY-4.0. I chose the Zenodo date as the first public written argument because the deposit's description says it carries the manuscript sources; I could not open the ZIP itself, so if the Zenodo v1.5.2 manuscript turns out not to contain the proofs, the date would be 18 May 2026.
events.revisions: Zenodo versions v1.5.2 (record 19644188), v1.5.3 (19644259), v2.0.0 (19645441) and v2.0.1 (19645478), all dated 18 Apr 2026. arXiv v1 18 May 2026, the only arXiv version seen; no v2 listed.
events.delivers: Primality of three specific Wagstaff numbers: exponents 2617, 10501 and 12391, each by an unconditional BLS N-1 proof with APR-CL on cofactors. The paper also states that all W_p with p <= 42737 have been proved prime or composite and that further exponents are probable primes; that is the author's compilation of existing status, not a result of this paper. Restricted to three exponents. It says nothing about any other exponent and nothing about whether infinitely many Wagstaff primes exist.
events.remains: The whole problem: whether infinitely many Wagstaff primes exist. Also every exponent other than 2617, 10501 and 12391, including the probable-prime exponents.

checked_by.who: Re-verifier script verify_bls.py bundled in the Zenodo deposit, written by the author
checked_by.qualification: Written by the author; not an independent party

events.time_since_posted: About 6 months since the Zenodo deposit (18 Apr 2026); about 5 months since arXiv v1 (18 May 2026). Two searches for public engagement or citations found none.
events.directly_checkable: The certificates are JSON files in the Zenodo deposit (data/). They can be re-checked by the bundled verify_bls.py or by running PARI/GP isprime(x, 2) on the cofactors. I have not seen an independent re-run.
events.doubts: No specific error identified. Points to weigh: (1) The Prime Pages entry for W_10501 (exponent 10501, t5k id 29287) already lists it as 'Proven' with a 2023-03-13 verification record of BLS N-1 ('[N-1/N+1, Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge]', N-1 step at 204.60% proof), while the paper says the author is 'not aware of previously published BLS N-1 proofs' for W_10501. A database record is not a publication, so this is a question of priority of record, not a contradiction; see disputes. (2) The arXiv HTML, as read through a summarising fetch tool, says '77 more probable primes' in section 1.1 while Appendix B.1 lists seven and the header total is 36; the 77 appears to be a typo for 7. (3) Single-author, no institutional affiliation; no public engagement found.
events.direction: Cuts neither way on the question. It certifies three exponents already on the known list as giving primes; it does not move the question of infinitude. Positive for the claim that these three Wagstaff numbers are prime.
events.object: BLS N-1 primality certificates in the Zenodo deposit for W_2617 = (2^2617+1)/3 (788 digits), W_10501 = (2^10501+1)/3 (3161 digits) and W_12391 = (2^12391+1)/3 (3730 digits). Each is an explicit proof of primality, not a non-constructive existence argument. These exponents are not new: 2617, 10501 and 12391 already appear in OEIS A000978 as Wagstaff exponents. Not a counterexample to anything.

events.what_happened: Stephen Marshall, 'Proof that Wagstaff Prime Numbers are Infinite', listed on viXra (an unrefereed preprint archive) with publication date 1 Apr 2019, per the sugaku.net aggregator. I could not open the viXra page or PDF: the viXra listing URLs returned 404 and the sugaku author and work pages returned 403, so the viXra identifier is unknown and the argument is unassessed. The aggregator lists the same author's similarly titled claims on Mersenne primes, Fermat primes and Sophie Germain primes, and claimed proofs of Goldbach and the Riemann hypothesis. The AI field below reflects that the listing names no AI; it does not reflect a reading of the paper.
events.delivers: If the title's claim is what the paper establishes, a proof that infinitely many primes of the form (2^p+1)/3 exist, which would settle the question. Content not verified; this is based on the title alone.
events.remains: Unknown. If the paper proves the title's claim, nothing; if not, everything.
events.time_since_posted: About 7.5 years (since 1 Apr 2019). viXra is not peer-reviewed; no review, citation or critique found in searches.
events.doubts: Not assessed. Reasons for caution that I can state: viXra is unrefereed; the same author's listing is a catalogue of similarly titled claims on other open problems; no public engagement found. The Groningen thesis (2024) reports that an attempted proof of infinitude is incorrect but does not name the attempt, so whether it addresses this paper is not established.
events.direction: Claims infinitude, i.e. affirms the conjecture, if the title reflects the paper.

events.what_happened: Djurre Germ Sikkema, bachelor's thesis 'Probable primality testing for Wagstaff primes' (University of Groningen, Mathematics; supervisors J. Top and P. Kilicer), deposited 8 Aug 2024. The abstract covers several probable-prime tests for Wagstaff numbers, including the Lifchitz test, a derivation of Miller's test and a Lucas-Lehmer-based generalised test whose special cases include the Vrba and Gerbicz tests. Its final sentence, quoted from the abstract, is: 'Finally an argument is given on why an attempted proof on whether there exist infinitely many Wagstaff primes is incorrect.' The attempted proof is not named. The PDF body could not be decoded by the fetch tool, so this entry rests on the abstract alone.
events.delivers: No result on infinitude. Per the abstract, it reports that an unnamed argument for infinitude is flawed. It establishes no existence and no non-existence result.

checked_by.who: Thesis supervisors J. Top and P. Kilicer, University of Groningen
checked_by.qualification: Academic supervisors in the mathematics department
checked_by.what_they_did: Supervised the thesis, which was deposited in the university's student-thesis repository (approval not verified beyond deposit)

events.time_since_posted: About 2 years (Aug 2024). The thesis is the only engagement with an attempted proof that I found.
events.doubts: The attempted proof is unnamed in the abstract, so the thesis's refutation cannot be assessed from what I read. Whether it addresses Marshall (2019) is not established.
events.direction: Against the particular infinitude argument it addresses, which is not named. No bearing on whether infinitely many exist.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr., 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures', Journal of Integer Sequences vol. 28 (2025), article 25.7.2, published 4 Dec 2025. Abstract, verbatim: 'We discuss two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, an old one and a new one. Heuristic arguments support both conjectures.' The section headings in the PDF outline give the old one as the 1989 New Mersenne conjecture and the new one as 'Chen's Mersenne Conjecture of 2025'. The PDF body could not be decoded, so the entry rests on the abstract and the outline.
events.delivers: Heuristic support for two conjectures about Mersenne numbers. The 1989 conjecture has, as one of three conditions, that (2^p+1)/3 is prime; it predicts that no odd p satisfies all three conditions beyond a finite range. That is a claim about joint conditions, not an infinitude claim for Wagstaff primes.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the paper

events.direction: Neutral on the question. Supports conjectures about Mersenne numbers; does not assert or refute that infinitely many Wagstaff primes exist.

events.what_happened: Herbert Batte, 'On Wagstaff primes in the k-Lucas number sequence', arXiv:2602.20387, submitted 23 Feb 2026 (one version). Studies the Diophantine equation L_n^(k) = (2^p+1)/3 with p an odd prime. Per the abstract as read through the fetch tool: the only solutions are (n,k,p) in {(5,2,5), (6,4,7)} together with {(2,k,3): k >= 2}, proved with linear forms in logarithms and LLL reduction.
events.delivers: Finitely many coincidences between k-Lucas numbers and Wagstaff-form numbers, plus an infinite family with p = 3 and varying k. Confined to the k-Lucas sequence. Nothing on whether there are infinitely many Wagstaff primes.
events.time_since_posted: About 8 months (since 23 Feb 2026). No engagement found.
events.direction: Neutral on the question. A Diophantine finiteness result for a neighbouring family of numbers.

events.what_happened: A comment on OEIS A000978 by Thomas Ordowski, dated 13 Sep 2026, posts a conjecture about the least prime factors of Wagstaff numbers. Read only as summarised by the fetch tool; the exact statement was not verified.
events.delivers: Nothing proved. A conjecture about least prime factors of (2^p+1)/3, not about how many of these numbers are prime.

disputes.summary: Prime Pages lists W_10501 (exponent 10501, entry id 29287, submitted 1996) as 'Proven', with a 2023-03-13 verification record of BLS N-1 (N-1 step at 204.60% proof, labelled '[N-1/N+1, Brillhart-Lehmer-Selfridge]', proof code 'M : Morain'). Dolotov (April/May 2026) says he is 'not aware of previously published BLS N-1 proofs' for W_10501. A database verification record is not a publication, so this is an open question of priority of record, not a settled contradiction. An earlier fetch of the Top-20 page had given this row as 'cyclotomy'; the entry page says BLS, and I rely on the entry page.

Marshall's 2019 viXra preprint claims a proof that Wagstaff primes are infinite. The 2024 Groningen thesis says an argument shows an attempted proof of infinitude is incorrect, without naming it. Whether these are the same argument is not established, and I could not open the viXra text. Neither has been resolved by any source found.

Prime Pages describes its Top 5000 list as proven primes only, yet the PRP entry for (2^141079+1)/3 appears on it. The status of the Wikipedia infobox's 'largest known term' (2^138937+1)/3, which dates to October 2023, is out of date relative to the 2025 entry (2^141079+1)/3, which Wikipedia's probable-prime list already includes.

summary: Searched the question of whether infinitely many Wagstaff primes exist, from the Wikipedia article and its raw wikitext, OEIS A000978, Prime Pages entries, arXiv, the Journal of Integer Sequences, Zenodo and GitHub, a Groningen thesis repository, and a blog. Both the Wikipedia article and OEIS describe the question as open: Wikipedia states the infinitude as a conjecture only for the more general Q(b,n) and gives no heuristic for b = 2, and I found no source claiming a settlement in either direction. In-window (after 26 Jan 2024) items are: the Groningen bachelor's thesis (Aug 2024), whose abstract says an unnamed attempted proof of infinitude is flawed; Wagstaff's JIS paper (Dec 2025) on two Mersenne-number conjectures, whose abstract does not mention Wagstaff primes; Batte's arXiv paper (Feb 2026) solving a Diophantine equation between k-Lucas numbers and Wagstaff-form numbers, giving finitely many coincidences; Dolotov's Zenodo and arXiv papers (Apr/May 2026) certifying W_2617, W_10501 and W_12391 as prime, all already on the known exponent list; and computational probable-prime entries (141079 in Oct 2025; OEIS comment by Ordowski, Sep 2026, on least prime factors). The pre-window Marshall viXra preprint (2019) claims a proof of infinitude; I could not open its text and found no engagement with it, so whether it has any merit is unassessed. The date for Dolotov's paper was a close call: I used the Zenodo deposit date (18 Apr 2026) because its description says it carries the manuscript sources, while arXiv v1 is 18 May 2026; I could not open the ZIP to confirm the deposit's contents. The AI search found nothing connecting any system to Wagstaff primes. The AI-related prime-theory items I did see (an OpenAI problem list with no Wagstaff entry, GPT-5 Erdős-problem work, an Axiom 'partially regular primes' paper, a claimed GPT-5.6 prime-gap record, Anthropic's Riemann-zeta bound of Aug 2026, OpenAI's May 2026 unit-distance disproof, and an unverified DeepMind 'prime pattern' headline) are about other problems. Dolotov's full HTML text was read through a summarising fetch tool and contains no AI mention; the Zenodo record states none exists. The Sikkema PDF and the Batte and JIS PDF bodies could not be decoded, so their AI-negative findings rest on abstracts and landing pages.
competing_reading: Reading 1: Dolotov's three certifications, plus the Prime Pages and OEIS probable-prime entries, count as in-window progress because each is a new certified or probable Wagstaff prime and the known set grows. Reading 2: infinitude is an existence claim that depends on unboundedly many instances, so a few more certified or probable primes move nothing, and the only candidate that would settle the question is a proof of infinitude, which none of the in-window items gives. I side with Reading 2 for the in-window items on the grounds of the scope rules, but I record both. For Marshall (2019), the strongest case for treating it as relevant is that its title claims exactly the bullet's answer; the strongest case against is that nothing supports its argument and its author's catalogue of similarly titled claims is a reason for caution.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The viXra text of Marshall's paper (identifier unknown; the viXra listing was not reachable), checked for the key step that would give infinitude, and whether the Groningen thesis's 'attempted proof' refers to it (the thesis PDF body, which the fetch tool could not decode). (2) A human reading or an independent re-run of Dolotov's certificates (the Zenodo ZIP, and the verify_bls.py re-verifier), and the Zenodo v1.5.2 ZIP contents, to confirm the 18 Apr 2026 date. (3) The Prime Pages maintainers' view on the 2023 BLS record for W_10501 versus Dolotov's priority claim. (4) A recent survey, or the current Wikipedia text, stating the status of infinitude for b = 2. None of these was available to me.
